title: Fertile adulthood from a vertebrate cell line, with no gestational parent

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a continuous route from a cultured vertebrate stem-cell line to a fertile adult, with no gestational parent involved in producing that founder animal. In the proposed mouse demonstration, all embryonic and extraembryonic cellular components would derive from one diploid stem-cell line. Development would proceed entirely outside a living uterus, without taking a gamete from an adult. The resulting animal would survive to adulthood and demonstrate reproductive competence through ordinary mating. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The experimental foundation is the ability of embryonic stem cells and extraembryonic stem cells to organize together into models that reproduce substantial early mouse development. Extraembryonic tissues help support and coordinate development alongside the embryo itself. Amadei and colleagues demonstrated gastrulation, neurulation and early organogenesis in such assemblies, approximately equivalent to embryonic day 8.5, or E8.5. The innovation would require extending this coordinated process through all remaining development and the transition to independent life.

significance.text: Conditional on success, this would establish a major new route to animal production: a cultured cell line could produce a fertile individual without adult-derived gametes or uterine gestation during founder production. Its revolutionary feature would be continuity across the entire developmental sequence. Early organization, a beating structure or an isolated organ would become steps within a process demonstrated to yield an independently living, reproductively competent animal.

It would also extend experimental access across development in the demonstrated species, potentially allowing researchers to manipulate genes, tissues and culture conditions at stages ordinarily difficult to observe or intervene in directly. The existing embryo-model work provides a concrete foundation for this prospect: Amadei and colleagues reproduced developmental consequences of Pax6 disruption in neurulating models. Nevertheless, development outside a parent would not automatically reproduce every aspect of natural development. Physiological and developmental fidelity would need separate assessment, even if the resulting animals were fertile.

A conditional conservation application would be producing an individual from a preserved or biopsied cell line, provided that suitable reprogramming and species-specific developmental methods were available. Producing one individual would not by itself establish a genetically diverse, self-sustaining breeding population. The 2026 interview discusses restoration-related possibilities while emphasizing that applications remain distant; it does not demonstrate this conservation pathway.

Scope synthesis: a successful mouse demonstration would establish the capability in mice. Transfer to endangered mammals, birds or fish could require substantial additional biological discoveries as well as engineering. Likewise, producing an animal from a chemically synthesized genome would require a separate genome-origin capability. IVF, cloning into a surrogate and stem-cell-derived gametes followed by uterine transfer would remain distinct because each retains a reproductive input or gestational step excluded by the proposed founder-production criterion.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is continuous, coordinated development from cultured stem cells to a fertile adult outside a gestational parent. The supplied primary study establishes only an early developmental foundation. Its limitations include abnormal or missing extraembryonic populations, incomplete organ development and constraints imposed by culture. These are obstacles within early development as well as barriers to later progression; the remaining problem cannot be reduced to supplying an artificial uterus after an otherwise complete early embryo has formed.

Placental and maternal-interface physiology are especially important for the proposed mouse route. An external system would have to provide the support normally obtained through those interfaces while maintaining developmentally appropriate interactions among embryonic and extraembryonic tissues. In the 2026 interview, Ding Sheng attributes developmental limits partly to culture conditions that fail to reproduce the maternal uterine interface. This is an attributed explanation in a secondary source, not a demonstration that a particular replacement system would solve the problem.

Engineering synthesis: a complete system would need to sustain changing requirements for nutrient delivery, gas exchange, waste removal and developmental signaling while organs mature together. It would also need to support the transition from external developmental support to independent circulation, respiration and feeding. A beating heart-like structure does not establish adequate circulation, and the presence of primordial germ cells does not establish mature gamete production or adult fertility.

Provenance synthesis: the proposed single-line route adds a requirement beyond assembling separately established embryonic and extraembryonic stem-cell populations. All necessary cellular lineages would have to be generated from the starting line with sufficient developmental competence and coordinated behavior. Success in one vertebrate would not establish that equivalent starting states, supporting tissues or culture conditions can be produced in another.

current_state.text: In the Nature paper published online on 25 August 2022, Amadei and colleagues assembled mouse embryonic stem cells, trophoblast stem cells and induced extraembryonic-endoderm stem cells into embryo models approximately equivalent to E8.5. The reported structures included brain regions, a beating heart-like structure, somites, a developing gut and primordial germ cells. The work demonstrated progression through gastrulation into neurulation and early organogenesis. It did not report birth or fertile adulthood, and its comparison with natural embryos included developmental differences and incomplete structures.

The supplied review assessed the retained scientific text, including the main results, discussion and methods. That extraction was partial: it was truncated in the references, and figures and videos were not independently inspected. These limits do not negate the dated textual report, but they constrain the assessment to the material reviewed and do not constitute an independent examination of every experimental artifact.

A 21 October 2026 article in The Paper described chemically induced totipotent stem cells and named a Nature paper. Its introductory framing referred broadly to E8.5–E10.5 equivalence. Within the interview, however, Ding Sheng specified overall model development to E8.5, with individual tissues or organs resembling approximately day 10. Consequently, the supplied report does not justify describing the whole model as having reached E10.5.

The complete secondary interview was available to the supplied review, but the primary paper it named was absent from the supplied evidence. The newer scientific result therefore remains unverified here at the primary-source level. This is an access limitation, not evidence that the reported result is false. Even the broader introductory staging claim would leave later development, birth, adult survival and fertility unestablished.

Evidence-scope synthesis: neither supplied source demonstrates external development from a stem-cell line through birth and fertile adulthood. However, no bounded freshness-search record was supplied, so this record cannot establish that the capability remained absent throughout the literature as of 1 November 2026. The dated 2022 achievement and the qualified 2026 secondary report should be distinguished from that unresolved question about the wider field.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed core demonstration: begin with a documented diploid mouse stem-cell line and derive all embryonic and extraembryonic cellular components from that line. Without taking a gamete from an adult and without any uterine gestation during founder production, the system should yield an animal that transitions to independent life, survives to adulthood and produces fertile offspring through ordinary mating. Ordinary mating is a subsequent fertility test and may involve uterine gestation; the no-uterus condition applies to producing the founder.
completion_criteria.label: Single-line mouse founders produce fertile offspring after entirely extrauterine development

completion_criteria.text: Proposed provenance and reproducibility requirements: document the starting line, lineage derivations, culture and support stages, and the complete developmental history of each founder. Genetic checks should establish the intended cellular origin and exclude unreported cellular contributions. Report outcomes for all initiated assemblies, including failures and abnormalities, so that a successful animal can be interpreted alongside the process's efficiency and reliability. Repeated success and independent reproduction would provide stronger evidence than a single exceptional outcome. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established completion standards.
completion_criteria.label: Document founder provenance and outcomes for all initiated assemblies

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional assessment: evaluate growth, major organ function, health and reproductive competence rather than relying only on embryonic morphology. Demonstrating that the founder's offspring are themselves fertile would directly test the stated requirement for fertile offspring. Adult fertility would be decisive for the central capability, but would not alone establish normal lifespan, absence of subtle developmental abnormalities or complete equivalence to naturally developed animals.
completion_criteria.label: Assess founder growth, physiological function and health; demonstrate offspring fertility

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: specify the genetic backgrounds, stem-cell states, culture conditions and support apparatus under which the method works, together with reproducibility and failure rates. One species would establish a species-specific capability. Additional lines, backgrounds and vertebrate species would demonstrate increasing breadth; finite demonstrations would not establish literal universality. Transfer to birds or fish should remain a separate research objective with uncertain biological and engineering requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Report operating conditions, reproducibility and failure rates within demonstrated scope

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ZOO-01, “A fertile animal booted from a chemically synthesized genome,” overlaps in its fertile-animal endpoint but asks a different question about the origin of the genome. ZOO-10 concerns the developmental route from a cell line without a gestational parent. A combined achievement could satisfy both, but a ZOO-10 demonstration using an existing genome would not establish ZOO-01, and the supplied material does not establish that either capability requires the other.

Roster-based synthesis: ZOO-04, “Self-sustaining populations reconstructed from extinct animal species,” could potentially use a cell-line-to-animal route as one component. Its population-level objective additionally requires suitable biological material, genetic diversity, reproduction and ecological persistence. ZOO-10 would establish individual production in the demonstrated species, not extinct-species reconstruction or a self-sustaining population.

Roster-based synthesis: ZOO-08, “Experimental origin of animal multicellular development,” shares an interest in how cells coordinate into developing organisms. ZOO-10 starts with a vertebrate cell line and seeks completion of an existing organismal developmental program; it would not by itself demonstrate the experimental origin of animal multicellular development. ZOO-09, “A heritable body plan the ancestor never had,” concerns inherited anatomical novelty. Completing development from a cell line does not require or demonstrate such novelty.

Roster-based synthesis: ZOO-02, “Complete limb regeneration in an adult mammal,” concerns rebuilding a structure within an existing adult, whereas ZOO-10 concerns whole-organism development. ZOO-03, “Negligible senescence as an installed life-history program,” concerns aging after development; reaching fertile adulthood would not establish negligible senescence. ZOO-07, “Reversible whole-animal biostasis,” concerns suspending and restoring an existing animal's functions, rather than sustaining development from cells.

Roster-based synthesis: ZOO-06, “A germline-transmitted photosynthetic organelle in an animal,” concerns a particular inherited cellular innovation; fertility in ZOO-10 would not demonstrate organelle installation or transmission. ZOO-05, “Two-way semantic communication with another animal species,” concerns communication rather than reproductive development. Neither is an established prerequisite or consequence of the proposed ZOO-10 capability.

unresolved_issues: The primary scientific basis of the 21 October 2026 interview remains unverified in the supplied evidence, including the exact methods, developmental staging and reproducibility.
The supplied material does not establish whether later peer-reviewed work had achieved the target capability by 1 November 2026.
It remains unknown whether one diploid stem-cell line can supply every necessary embryonic and extraembryonic cellular component with sufficient competence for continuous external development.
The external support requirements for later mouse development, transition to independent life and reliable adult fertility remain unresolved.
Practical success rates, long-term health, developmental fidelity and transferability across genetic backgrounds or species are not established.
The roster permits a conceptual distinction between ZOO-01 and ZOO-10, but their technical dependencies cannot be resolved from titles alone.

brief.title: Fertile animals grown entirely outside a parent
possible: Researchers could grow a fertile mouse entirely outside a living parent, starting with a single stem-cell line, a population of cultured cells that can form different tissues. The line would supply both the animal and its supporting tissues, without eggs or sperm taken from an adult. The mouse would grow to adulthood and produce fertile offspring through ordinary mating.
why: Researchers could observe and alter development through stages usually hidden inside a parent. They could study how genes, tissues and growing organs work together across the whole process of making an animal.

sources.showed: They assembled mouse stem cells into embryo models that developed brain regions, a beating heart-like structure and a developing gut. Development reached roughly the equivalent of embryonic day 8.5.
sources.quote: This complete embryo model develops within an extraembryonic yolk sac that initiates blood island development.
sources.cited_for: Stem cells can organize into an early mouse embryo model with several developing organs.
sources.not_established: The models had incomplete structures and developmental differences, and did not reach birth or fertile adulthood.

sources.who: Ding Sheng and colleagues at Tsinghua University
sources.showed: In an interview, Ding reported that chemically induced stem cells developed continuously into mouse embryo models reaching the equivalent of embryonic day 8.5. He also reported abnormal cells during later development.
sources.quote: 我们在单细胞测序中也观察到，发育后期除了正常胚胎应有的细胞外，还出现了一小部分不和谐的、正常胚胎没有的“中间态细胞”。
sources.cited_for: A chemically induced starting cell can support continuous early development into a mouse embryo model.
sources.not_established: The reported models stopped during early development, leaving full external development and adult fertility unestablished.

shown: Amadei and colleagues grew assembled mouse stem cells into embryo models with early organs. Ding Sheng’s team later reported a chemically induced starting cell reaching a similar overall stage. Both reached roughly the equivalent of embryonic day 8.5.
missing: A single starting cell line must supply every cell type needed for the animal and its supporting tissues.
External support must sustain coordinated organ growth while delivering nutrients and oxygen, removing waste and providing developmental signals.
An animal must complete external development, begin breathing and feeding independently, and survive to fertile adulthood.

milestones.label: A fully externally grown mouse produces fertile offspring
milestones.explanation: A mouse cell line with paired chromosomes would have to supply all cells for an independently living adult that produces fertile offspring by mating. This would establish the route without adult eggs, sperm or pregnancy during its production.

milestones.label: Cell origins and every developmental outcome are documented
milestones.explanation: Genetic checks and complete developmental histories would have to establish cell origins and outcomes for every started assembly, including failures and abnormalities. Repeated success would establish reliability.

milestones.label: Adult health and offspring fertility are demonstrated
milestones.explanation: Assessments would have to measure adult growth, major organ function, health and reproduction, including fertility of the offspring. These would establish function beyond an embryo’s appearance.

milestones.label: Working conditions and failure rates are established
milestones.explanation: Results would have to specify genetic backgrounds, cell states, culture conditions, support equipment, repeatability and failure rates. These would define where the method works and how reliably.

uncertain: It remains unknown whether a single cell line can provide every required cell type with the ability to sustain full development.
The support needed for later development and the transition to independent life remains unresolved.
Long-term health, subtle developmental differences and transfer to other genetic backgrounds or species remain open questions.

page.title: Complete ectogenesis from a mouse stem-cell line
page.definition: A mouse develops from one diploid stem-cell line into a fertile adult through complete ectogenesis: development entirely outside a living uterus. The line supplies the animal and its extraembryonic tissues, which support development, without eggs or sperm collected from adults to produce the founder.

goal.need: Mouse gestation lasts approximately 19–21 days. Stem-cell embryo models reported on 25 August 2022 and 14 October 2026 reproduced development resembling embryonic day 8.5; the later paper's day-10.5 comparison concerned cardiac tissue. Extending this access through birth and reproduction would allow developmental perturbations to be followed from cultured cells into a reproducing animal.

statements.quote: a useful model system for studying factors affecting embryonic development.
statements.context: NIH describes the research purpose of early mouse stem-cell embryo models.

statements.body: Sheng Ding's team, School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Tsinghua University
statements.quote: 因此，十多年前我提出的概念是，能不能获得“生命”，而不是获得“细胞”？
statements.context: Ding describes his motivating question as whether one can obtain life, rather than cells. The interview concerns mouse chemically induced totipotent-like stem cells and supplies no fertility threshold.

completion.title: A mouse from one stem-cell line completes extrauterine development and produces live offspring.
completion.criterion: One mouse is produced entirely outside a living uterus from one diploid stem-cell line supplying all embryonic and extraembryonic cells, without adult-derived eggs or sperm during founder production. It survives to at least eight weeks after transition to postnatal life and produces live offspring through ordinary mating, with genetic parentage established. Postnatal fostering and uterine gestation of its offspring are allowed. This is an Atlas operational test; the IMPC supplies the minimum mating-test age, not an ectogenesis standard.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational definition; no external body was found to have published this combined test.
completion.basis: Checks of ISSCR guidance, mouse embryo-model protocols and IMPC fertility criteria, and searches for ectogenesis standards, prizes and roadmaps found no external end-to-end test combining single-line origin, entirely extrauterine development and fertility. The Atlas test therefore requires one founder that reproduces, without adding an efficiency target; eight weeks is the IMPC's minimum fertility-testing age.

milestones.title: A mouse stem-cell embryo model forms headfolds and a beating heart-like region by culture day 8.
milestones.criterion: At culture day 8, a mouse stem-cell embryo model has distinct regions resembling headfolds, beating heart, tail, allantois and chorion, meeting the published protocol's morphological endpoint. Amadei et al., 25 August 2022: day-8 morphology included 40 models in a developmental series spanning 17 experiments. Wu et al., 14 October 2026: whole models resembled E8.5 embryos; E10.5 equivalence concerned cardiac tissue (late-model images: 3 models from 3 experiments). Neither result demonstrates adulthood.
milestones.set_by: Lau, Amadei and Zernicka-Goetz, Nature Protocols, step 67; the criterion was written for EiTiX mouse embryo models assembled from embryonic stem-cell populations.
milestones.threshold_quote: Successful Day 8 EiTiX embryos should have distinctive regions resembling more developed headfolds, beating heart, tail, allantois and chorion.

milestones.title: A stem-cell-derived mouse embryo reaches Theiler stage 18 outside a uterus.
milestones.criterion: A stem-cell-derived mouse embryo develops outside a uterus to Theiler stage 18: progressive lens-vesicle closure, nasal-pit formation and 40–44 somite pairs. This corresponds approximately to embryonic day 11, not 11 days of culture. Supporting result: Aguilera-Castrejon et al., 17 March 2021, cultured natural E5.5 embryos for six days to 42 somites; endpoint images represented at least three embryos. Those embryos had developed in a uterus before explantation.
milestones.set_by: Theiler staging, reproduced in EMAP's mouse-development atlas, Appendix I; the anatomical stage was defined for natural mouse embryos.

milestones.title: A stem-cell-derived mouse reaches the late fetal anatomy of Theiler stage 26 outside a uterus.
milestones.criterion: A stem-cell-derived mouse develops outside a uterus to Theiler stage 26, approximately embryonic day 18: elongated whiskers, thickened skin, enlarged external ears covering almost all the ear-canal opening, and eyes barely visible through closed eyelids. This is an anatomical endpoint; it does not establish postnatal survival.
milestones.set_by: Theiler staging, reproduced in EMAP's mouse-development atlas, Appendix I; the anatomical stage was defined for natural mouse fetuses.
milestones.threshold_quote: The whiskers that were present at stage 25 are definitely longer and the skin has thickened.

milestones.title: A mouse produced without uterine gestation survives to weaning at approximately 21 days.
milestones.criterion: A mouse produced by entirely extrauterine development survives the neonatal period to weaning at approximately 21 postnatal days, or up to 28 days under the Jackson Laboratory convention. Postnatal fostering is compatible with this endpoint.
milestones.set_by: The Jackson Laboratory, Colony Planning; the published weaning-age convention concerns laboratory mice generally.
milestones.threshold_quote: Wean age: ~21 days; up to 28 days if preferred

milestones.title: A mouse produced without uterine gestation survives to the IMPC mating-test age of eight weeks.
milestones.criterion: A mouse produced by entirely extrauterine development survives to at least eight postnatal weeks, the minimum age specified for entry into the IMPC fertility protocol. This establishes survival to the age of the reproductive test; producing offspring is the completion criterion.
milestones.set_by: International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium, IMPReSS protocol IMPC_FER_001; the protocol concerns homozygous knockout mice, and its minimum testing age supplies this survival endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: Minimal age at test = minimal age at start of procedure = 8 weeks.

not_found: No external completion criterion combining single-line origin, entirely extrauterine development and adult fertility was found in searches of guidance, standards, prizes and ectogenesis roadmaps.
No report of a mouse completing that combined route was located in searches of stem-cell embryo and ex utero development literature through 14 November 2026.
The 2026 Nature article's main text was subscription-restricted; its abstract and extended-data captions were accessible.
